description: Just a team looking to try and win a hackathon.
summary:
ASTRA is a web app that lets anyone check whether something in the infrared sky really moved or changed, using real SPHEREx data. Type a star's name or coordinates. ASTRA pulls every public SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 exposure of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, stacks them into visits about six months apart, and lets you blink them, the way Pluto was found on photographic plates in 1930. It measures position, brightness, a 0.75–5 µm spectrum and proper motion, then checks the result against Gaia, SIMBAD, CatWISE and known asteroids.

The hard part of finding faint moving objects is false positives: saturated stars, detector artifacts, blended neighbours and out-of-date coordinates. ASTRA puts the evidence for and against every result on screen, grades confidence with written rules instead of invented percentages, and says "motion not measured" when the data cannot support a claim. An optional AI explainer only restates measured evidence and cannot add numbers. On Eps Indi B it recovers the brown dwarf's motion within 0.6σ of Gaia; on four harder targets it explains exactly why it cannot. ASTRA never announces discoveries: it hands unexplained changes to people for review.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRA turns SPHEREx's 102-colour infrared sky survey into investigations anyone can run. For any sky position it:

1. Resolves a name or coordinates and carries the object's catalogue motion forward to today (the challenge's WISE 0855 coordinates are its ~2010 position, about 2 arcmin from where it is now).

2. Finds every SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 exposure of that spot through IRSA's SIA2 service and downloads small calibrated cutouts, with the zodiacal light model removed.

3. Stacks exposures into visits about six months apart. You can play, blink and difference them like a time-lapse, shown as photographic negatives with the predicted track drawn on.

4. Measures aperture photometry, centroids, a 0.75–5 µm spectrum, a light curve and a proper-motion fit (parallax too, when the visits allow).

5. Checks everything: SPHEREx artifact flags, saturation, blends with neighbouring Gaia stars, and cross-matches with Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, CatWISE and SkyBoT (known asteroids).

6. Grades the result with written rules into four tiers (insufficient, low, moderate, strong). Every evidence item shows its value, threshold and reason.

7. Optionally explains the evidence in plain language with Google Gemini. Each sentence is tagged as measured, catalogue, interpretation or hypothesis, and a validator rejects any number that is not in the evidence. Without AI, a fixed template is used.

8. Lets people record verdicts in a review queue, export reports, and share any view by URL.

VALIDATION ON KNOWN TARGETS

We ran the five challenge targets, where the right answer is known:

- Eps Indi B: motion measured, 0.6σ from the Gaia value; free-fit parallax within 1σ.

- WISE 0855: motion not measured, because a brighter Gaia star 7.2″ away dominates the position. Before we added the blend check, this showed up as a fake 21σ disagreement.

- Barnard's Star and R Dra: saturated in 99% of exposures, so ASTRA declines to measure.

- RW Aur: known variable, matched in SIMBAD.

A tool that reported confident detections here would be wrong. ASTRA reports why it cannot tell.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Searches for Planet X-style objects are faint, cold, moving-object searches, and almost every apparent signal is something else. ASTRA shows the full chain from pixels to conclusion, including the reasons a signal might not be real. That makes it both a teaching tool for students and citizen scientists and a quick vetting tool for anyone checking a candidate. It works on any position on the sky, live on the public archive, and gets better on its own as each new SPHEREx release adds visits.

TOOLS

Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Astropy, photutils, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, httpx. Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Plotly.js, Aladin Lite v3. Optional explainer: Google Gemini API. Hosting: Render (API) and Vercel (web app).

CREATIVITY

The interface borrows from how Pluto was actually found: astronomers blinked two photographic plates and looked for the speck that jumped. ASTRA shows SPHEREx images as plate negatives, marks measurements in red pencil, blinks visits like a blink comparator, and lets you look through a loupe at the sky behind the page. The goal is that the method is visible, not hidden behind a score.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty over impressiveness: no fake percentages, no "discovery" claims. Archive outages are reported as outages, not as "no match".

- Real data only. The decorative plate background is labelled as an illustration, and survey images from other telescopes are labelled as context, not SPHEREx data.

- Known limits, stated openly: aperture photometry (not PSF fitting), simple image differencing, and only 4–5 visits so far, so no period searches and wide motion errors.

- ASTRA is an independent project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
